title: Zapier Advanced: Code Steps, Custom API Calls, and Sub-Zaps
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Zapier Advanced: Code Steps, Custom API Calls, and Sub-Zaps ##### The ceiling that turned out to be a door A consultant told a client that Zapier could not do the job. The client's inventory system had a REST API, but no Zapier integration existed. The client's requirement — deduplicate incoming SKUs against everything seen in the last 30 days — had no native action either. The recommendation was a three-week n8n migration. A second opinion took ninety minutes. **Custom Request** hit the inventory API directly. **Storage by Zapier** held the seen-SKU set. **Code by Zapier** did the normalization. The Zap shipped that afternoon and is still running. Zapier's reputation as "the simple one" is earned at the surface and misleading underneath. Its escape hatches — code steps, raw HTTP, storage, sub-zaps — cover far more ground than most users realize. Knowing where the actual ceiling sits, rather than the apparent one, is what lets you choose tools on merit instead of assumption. ##### Code by Zapier The Code step runs JavaScript (Node) or Python in a sandbox. It is the general-purpose escape hatch for logic that would otherwise take six Formatter steps — or that no Formatter can express. The contract is specific and worth memorizing: - **Input** — you explicitly declare key/value pairs in the "Input Data" section, mapped from earlier steps. They arrive as `inputData` (JS) or `input_data` (Python). Nothing is available unless you map it — a deliberate design that makes dependencies visible. - **Everything arrives as a string.** Numbers, booleans, dates: all strings. Coerce explicitly. - **Output** — return an object for one downstream item, or an array of objects to **fan out**, causing all subsequent steps to run once per element. - **Limits** — roughly 10 seconds runtime (1 second on free plans), 128 MB memory, no npm packages, though `fetch` is available in JS. ```javascript // Code by Zapier — JavaScript // Input Data: rawItems (JSON string), currency, orderId const items = JSON.parse(inputData.rawItems || "[]"); const cleaned = items .filter(i => i.status !== "cancelled") .map(i => { const qty = parseInt(i.nights, 10) || 0; const rate = parseFloat(String(i.rate).replace(/[^0-9.]/g, "")) || 0; return { sku: String(i.sku || "").trim().toUpperCase(), qty, rate, lineTotal: Math.round(qty * rate * 100) / 100, }; }); const subtotal = cleaned.reduce((s, i) => s + i.lineTotal, 0); // Returning an ARRAY fans out: later steps run once per line item. // Returning a single OBJECT keeps one execution. return { orderId: inputData.orderId, currency: inputData.currency || "INR", lineCount: cleaned.length, subtotal: Math.round(subtotal * 100) / 100, tax: Math.round(subtotal * 0.18 * 100) / 100, total: Math.round(subtotal * 1.18 * 100) / 100, itemsJson: JSON.stringify(cleaned), // pass structured data forward as a string hasCancellations: items.length !== cleaned.length, }; ``` That fan-out behaviour is the most powerful and most surprising property. Returning an array is Zapier's closest equivalent to Make's Iterator — and it means each downstream action costs a task **per item**, which you must factor into cost estimates. Two production habits: pass structured data between steps as a JSON string and parse it on the other side, since Zapier flattens nested objects unhelpfully; and wrap risky parsing in `try/catch`, returning an `error` field rather than throwing, so a malformed record produces a routable outcome instead of a halted Zap. ##### Custom Request: raw HTTP **Webhooks by Zapier → Custom Request** is a full HTTP client as an action step. Method, URL, headers, query params, and a raw body. This means **any REST API is integrable**, whether or not Zapier has built an app for it. Configuration that matters: - **Method and URL**, with mapped fields interpolated into the path. - **Data** — the raw request body. Set it to raw JSON and add `Content-Type: application/json` in headers, otherwise Zapier form-encodes and the API rejects it. - **Headers** — `Authorization: Bearer {{token}}`, custom API-key headers, `Idempotency-Key`. - **Unflatten** — leave off when sending nested JSON, or Zapier will restructure your payload. ```json { "method": "POST", "url": "https://api.inventory-vendor.com/v2/stock-adjustments", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {{secret_token}}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": "adj-{{order_id}}" }, "data": "{\"sku\":\"{{sku}}\",\"delta\":-{{qty}},\"reason\":\"sale\",\"ref\":\"{{order_id}}\"}" } ``` That `Idempotency-Key` derived from the order ID is what makes Zapier's Autoreplay safe on this step — a replay sends the same key and the vendor deduplicates server-side. A caution on credentials: values typed into a Custom Request are stored in the Zap definition. Prefer Zapier's **Storage secrets** or a connected app's authentication where available, and never paste a production key into a Zap you will screenshot or share. ##### Storage by Zapier **Storage by Zapier** is a simple key–value store scoped to a secret store ID. It gives Zaps something they otherwise lack entirely: **memory across runs**. Actions available: Set Value, Get Value, Set Multiple, Get Many, Increment, Remove, Pop/Push on lists, and — critically — **Set Value If** (a conditional write) and **Get Value and Remove**. The deduplication pattern: ```text 1. Trigger new inventory record 2. Code by Zapier normalize → dedupeKey = `sku:${sku}:${yyyymm}` 3. Storage: Get Value key = dedupeKey 4. Filter only continue if step 3 value does not exist 5. ... do the real work ... 6. Storage: Set Value key = dedupeKey, value = timestamp ``` Two honest limitations. Storage is **eventually consistent and not transactional**, so a check-then-set race is possible under high concurrency — use *Set Value If* where atomicity matters, and prefer a real database for anything financial. And values are capped in size (a few KB), so store keys and flags, not payloads. Storage also solves **counters** (Increment for rate-limit budgets), **cursors** (last synced timestamp for a polling Zap), and **cross-Zap flags**. ##### Sub-Zaps **Sub-Zaps** bring functions to Zapier. A Sub-Zap has a *Start* trigger declaring named inputs, some steps, and a *Return* action declaring named outputs. Parent Zaps invoke it with **Call a Sub-Zap** and receive the outputs synchronously. Why this matters for maintainability: the shared notification-and-logging routine that appears in eleven Zaps becomes one Sub-Zap. Changing the Slack channel format is one edit instead of eleven — and, more importantly, there is no risk of the eleven copies drifting apart, which is what actually happens over eighteen months. ```mermaid flowchart LR P1[Parent Zap A
order paid] --> S{{Sub-Zap:
notify + log}} P2[Parent Zap B
refund issued] --> S S --> N[Format message
by severity] N --> SL[Slack post] SL --> LG[Append to log sheet] LG --> R[Return: logged_at, message_ts] R -.outputs.-> P1 R -.outputs.-> P2 ``` Good Sub-Zap candidates are the same as good function candidates: normalize a contact, find-or-create a CRM record, send a formatted notification, write a run-log row, classify text with AI. Design them with **explicit typed inputs and outputs** and no hidden dependencies on parent context. Constraints to plan around: Sub-Zaps run synchronously and count toward the parent's execution time; nesting depth is limited; and each Sub-Zap's steps consume tasks, so a Sub-Zap called from a fanned-out array multiplies quickly. ##### Error handling, Autoreplay, and monitoring Advanced Zapier reliability rests on four mechanisms: **Autoreplay** (paid plans) automatically retries Zaps that error on transient conditions, with backoff, for up to a few days. It is genuinely useful — and genuinely dangerous on non-idempotent actions. A `POST /charges` without an idempotency key that times out and autoreplays charges twice. **Enable Autoreplay only on steps you have made idempotent.** **Error handling paths.** Zapier halts a Zap at the first erroring step, so an alert step placed after the failure never runs. The workaround is to make risky steps *not error*: use a Custom Request (which returns the status code as data rather than throwing on 4xx), then branch on `status_code` with Paths — one path for success, one for failure that logs and alerts. **Zap monitoring.** Task History filtered by status; error notification emails; and the platform auto-disabling a Zap after repeated failures. Do not rely on the emails alone — build a monitoring Zap that reads your log sheet on a schedule and alerts when the success rate drops or when no runs have occurred in the expected window. **Versioning.** Zapier keeps Zap versions and lets you restore a previous one — the closest thing to Git available. Combine with a documented change note in the Zap description. ##### Choosing between the three escape hatches The assignment asks for this decision, and the ordering principle is the same as everywhere else — **simplest thing that works**: - **Native action first.** Auth, pagination, retries and field pickers are handled, and a non-technical colleague can maintain it. Use unless it genuinely cannot do the job. - **Custom Request** when the app has no Zapier integration, or the integration lacks the specific endpoint you need. You take on auth and error handling in exchange for reach. - **Code by Zapier** when the transformation exceeds Formatter: multi-field logic, array processing, deduplication keys, fan-out, or anything needing conditionals. Also when collapsing five Formatter steps into one saves four tasks per run. A cost note that often decides it: five Formatter steps at 10,000 runs a month is 50,000 tasks; one Code step is 10,000. On Zapier's pricing that difference is substantial and is frequently the strongest argument for a code step. ##### Common pitfalls - **Forgetting to map Input Data** — `inputData.foo` is undefined because you never declared it. - **Assuming types.** Everything is a string; `"3" + 4` is `"34"` in JavaScript. - **Returning an array unintentionally**, fanning out and multiplying task consumption. - **Nested JSON in Custom Request** without disabling Unflatten. - **Missing `Content-Type: application/json`**, causing form-encoding and a 400. - **Autoreplay on non-idempotent writes**, producing duplicates. - **Storage race conditions** under concurrent runs — use Set Value If or a database. - **Alert steps after the failing step**, which never execute. - **Sub-Zaps called inside a fan-out**, quietly multiplying tasks and runtime. - **Secrets pasted into Custom Request fields** and then shared in a screenshot. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task combines all three escape hatches in one Zap: a **Code step** that transforms data, a **Custom Request** hitting an endpoint with no native action, and **Storage by Zapier** deduplicating against previously seen IDs. Test the dedupe properly — send the same record three times and confirm exactly one downstream action fires. The mini project raises it to an architecture: a **reusable Sub-Zap** for a shared notification-and-logging routine, **called from two parent Zaps**, where at least one parent uses a **Custom Request** to an unsupported API and includes **Autoreplay-based error handling**. Make the Sub-Zap's interface explicit — document its inputs and outputs in the description — because that contract is what makes it safely reusable. For the assignment, explain **when to reach for Code by Zapier versus a Custom Request versus a native action**, and describe how **Sub-Zaps and Storage improve maintainability and correctness**. Include the cost dimension: task consumption is a legitimate engineering input on Zapier, and the ability to reason about it is precisely what distinguishes an intermediate practitioner. ##### Key takeaways - Zapier's real ceiling is much higher than its surface suggests: Code steps, Custom Request, Storage and Sub-Zaps cover most cases people migrate away for. - Code by Zapier takes explicitly mapped string inputs and returns an object — or an array, which fans out and multiplies task cost. - Custom Request makes any REST API reachable; set the content type, disable Unflatten for nested JSON, and add idempotency keys before enabling Autoreplay. - Storage by Zapier provides cross-run memory for deduplication, counters and cursors, but is size-limited and not transactional — use a database for anything financial. - Sub-Zaps are functions: extract shared routines with explicit inputs and outputs to prevent the copy-drift that ruins large Zapier estates.
